content: 1. The BTPTR regimen involves administering levofloxacin daily for six months as a preventive treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). The dosage is determined by the patient’s age and weight. For children under 15 years of age, the approximate dose is 15–20 mg/kg/day, using 100 mg dispersible tablets. Specific weight-based dosages are as follows: 5–<10 kg: 150 mg/day 10–<16 kg: 200–300 mg/day 16–<24 kg: 300–400 mg/day 24–<35 kg: 500–750 mg/day 2. For individuals aged 15 years and older, the dosage is based on body weight: <46 kg: 750 mg/day >45 kg: 1 g/day 3. Contacts of individuals with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) may be treated similarly to those exposed to MDR-TB. If the index patient is confirmed to be susceptible to isoniazid, contacts may receive 6H (six months of daily isoniazid) or 9H (nine months of daily isoniazid). 4. In cases where the index patient has isoniazid-resistant but rifampicin-susceptible TB, there is limited evidence to guide the choice of preventive treatment regimens. However, 4R (four months of daily rifampicin) may be considered as an option. 5. Aligning clinic visits for child or adolescent contacts with the care schedule of the index patient, especially when they belong to the same family, is an important consideration to ensure adherence and convenience. 6. Families may find it challenging to understand why a healthy child needs to take daily or weekly medication for 3–6 months to prevent TB disease. It is crucial to clearly explain the rationale for preventive treatment and emphasize the importance of adherence at every visit. 7. Children on TB preventive treatment (TPT) can be reviewed at home, with monthly supplies provided. In some settings, this can be coordinated with home-based treatment support for adult index patients. 8. If symptoms suggestive of TB disease develop (e.g., cough, fever, fatigue, poor weight gain, reduced playfulness), the child should be evaluated for TB disease. If breakthrough TB occurs while on TPT, the preventive treatment should be stopped, and TB treatment should be initiated. Specimens should be sent for diagnostic testing, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, Ultra, line probe assay (LPA), or drug susceptibility testing (DST), as appropriate. 9. Weight should be monitored regularly to ensure the correct TPT dosage and to detect any evidence of TB disease. Adverse events related to the prescribed TPT regimen should also be monitored and managed accordingly. 10. Adherence to TPT should be reinforced at every visit, and pill counts should be conducted. If adherence is poor or there are interruptions, healthcare workers should explore the reasons and discuss options with the child’s parent or guardian. Support for the family should be expressed, and any issues requiring referral or treatment should be addressed. 11. All children and adolescents on TPT should be registered to collect data on treatment uptake, adherence, and outcomes, including breakthrough TB. This information is essential for monitoring and ensuring the availability of medicines. 12. Adherence to TPT is influenced by various factors, including personal motivation, beliefs about health, perceived risks and benefits, comorbidities, family environment, treatment complexity, medication toxicity, and trust in healthcare providers. 13. Effective, person-centered strategies to promote adherence include ensuring confidentiality, providing clear information about TPT options and duration, involving family members in health education, and reinforcing supportive messages at each visit. 14. Caregivers should be educated on how to administer child-friendly formulations, such as dispersible tablets, and given clear instructions on dissolving the medicine in water. 15. For children refusing medication, strategies include masking the taste with different foods, offering rewards for completing doses, and ensuring a new dose is given if vomiting occurs within 30 minutes of administration. 16. Families should be provided with extra doses each month to account for potential losses, and programs should estimate such losses in procurement plans. Persistent vomiting requires consultation at a healthcare facility. 17. Adherence plans should be developed with caregivers and shared with other caregivers involved in the child’s care. These plans should be reviewed at each encounter, especially if a new caregiver is present. 18. Shorter TPT regimens are associated with better adherence and higher treatment completion rates. Completion criteria are based on taking at least 80% of the recommended doses within 133% of the planned treatment duration. 19. If treatment interruptions occur, the next steps depend on the duration of the interruption and the percentage of doses already taken. For interruptions of less than two weeks, treatment can be resumed immediately, with missed doses added to the total treatment duration. For longer interruptions, restarting the full TPT course may be necessary, depending on the circumstances. 20. Infection prevention and control measures are critical to reducing the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These include administrative controls (e.g., triage, isolation, prompt treatment), environmental controls (e.g., ventilation, ultraviolet germicidal systems), and respiratory protection (e.g., particulate respirators). 21. Adolescents aged 10–19 years pose a similar transmission risk as adults with TB, while children under 10 years are less likely to transmit the disease. However, infection control principles apply to all healthcare settings where children and their families seek care. 22. The COVID-19 pandemic has normalized mask-wearing in many settings, potentially reducing stigma and facilitating the implementation of cough etiquette and respiratory protection measures. 23. For further guidance on TPT in children and adolescents, including the management of adverse events, drug interactions, and monitoring, refer to the WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis.
